C001035.text: Thank you, @ChuckGrassley. As Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, I worked with colleagues on both sides of the aisle to craft this stopgap funding measure. After three unnecessary lapses in funding during the fiscal year 2026 cycle, putting the possibility of yet another harmful shutdown off the table should be a priority for each and every one of us.

Tonight on the Senate floor, I urged my colleagues to support the bipartisan continuing resolution I worked with members of both parties to craft as Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. After three unnecessary lapses in funding during the fiscal year 2026 cycle, putting the possibility of yet another harmful government shutdown off the table should be a priority for each and every one of us. This straightforward measure would keep the government funded through December 11, protect vital programs and services, and give Congress additional time to continue our work on bipartisan appropriations bills. We cannot allow another damaging shutdown to disrupt the lives of federal workers and the Americans who depend on their work.

Despite tight personal budgets, it is truly remarkable how often teachers in Maine and across the country use money out of their own pockets to purchase classroom supplies for their students. We are fortunate to have so many dedicated educators who make sacrifices to help ensure that every child has a learning environment that is safe, welcoming, and enriching. That is why I am proud to announce that the Senate today passed the Supporting Early-Childhood Educators’ Deductions (SEED) Act, a bipartisan bill I introduced with Senator Michael Bennet. The SEED Act would provide tax relief for millions of teachers by expanding the above-the-line $300 educator expense deduction, established for K-12 teachers in 2002, to include pre-K and early childhood educators. As the author of the original educator expense tax deduction for K-12 teachers, I am delighted to help lead this effort to expand this benefit to early childhood educators. We can never thank our teachers enough for all they do to prepare the next generation for success, but the Senate’s passage of this commonsense bill brings us one step closer to providing early childhood educators with well-deserved tax relief.

Today, the Senate unanimously passed my bipartisan bill with Senator Tina Smith to reauthorize the Kay Hagan Tick Act, which we first authored in 2019. Maine reported 4,257 cases of Lyme disease last year – more than three times the number of cases reported just six years ago – and 2026 is projected to set yet another record. This is a record that we do not want to set. Our bill will expand efforts to combat Lyme and other tick-borne diseases while supporting promising work already underway in Maine, including a clinical trial for a human Lyme disease vaccine at the MaineHealth Institute for Research and the University of Maine Tick Lab, where Mainers can submit ticks to be identified and tested for pathogens.

I have carefully reviewed Todd Blanche’s qualifications to be Attorney General. This includes his record and responses to questions from Senators at the Department of Justice Appropriations hearing, his confirmation hearing, and in the weeks that followed. While I believe Mr. Blanche is a capable lawyer, the Department of Justice has become increasingly political. Mr. Blanche has taken several actions that have further eroded the Department’s independence, and that is the basis for my vote to oppose his confirmation: Mr. Blanche approved an order to shield the President, his sons, and the family business from IRS audits, protections unavailable to other American taxpayers. He approved the creation of a $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund. He promised an anti-abortion organization that he would seek to prohibit the mailing of abortion medication to women nationwide. Under his leadership, the Department attempted to indict Senators Mark Kelly and Elissa Slotkin over their ill-advised, but constitutionally protected, videos encouraging resistance to unlawful orders. More than 1,200 former Department of Justice employees have opposed his nomination, arguing that he has undermined the institution. For these reasons, I will vote against this nomination.

B000490.text: This week, the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, appeared before the U.S. House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services and General Government. During the hearing, I asked the Director about how Congress can be any clearer to ensure that the Trump Administration understands that once a funding bill is signed into law, the President is not allowed to change or second-guess the spending and withhold it due to policy or political differences. That is at the heart of Article 1 of the U.S. Constitution and why Congress also passed the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, when President Nixon tried to withhold funds that were already obligated according to the law.

This week, I asked the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, to explain how poorly planned cuts to the federal workforce last year have weakened services and protections upon which Americans rely. This includes the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, which is responsible for protecting America’s agriculture from invasive species and diseases. USDA-APHIS began mounting a vigorous response to the resurgence of New World Screwworm – a deadly parasite affecting livestock – in 2024. However, in early 2025, the Administration illegally fired workers and forced others to resign, causing over 25 percent of all USDA-APHIS employees to leave. USDA’s New World Screwworm prevention, monitoring, surveillance, and control efforts were halted. USDA had approved $378 million in prevention and control funding for sterile fly facilities in 2023 and 2024, yet the money went unspent when the new administration paused funding. This is extremely concerning to our ranchers, and this outbreak could drive the price of food even higher. Unfortunately, we continue to see the fallout of the blunt and ill-considered cuts to federal workers, from the return of New World Screwworm to the United States, to farmers showing up to closed or understaffed Farm Service Agency offices, to attacks on our nuclear safety programs putting national security at risk. I will continue to hold the White House accountable, as I did this week during the U.S. House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services and General Government hearing with Mr. Vought.

It is with heartfelt sadness that I learned of the passing of my dear friend, and magnificent former colleague, Kay Granger of Fort Worth, Texas. Some simply hold the gavel – Kay demonstrated what it meant to wield it. Her life and career were defined by a remarkable legacy of firsts: the first woman to become Mayor of Fort Worth, the first Republican woman elected to Congress from Texas, the first woman to Chair the Appropriations Defense Subcommittee, and the first woman to lead House Republicans on the Appropriations Committee. Yet, Kay never rested in the remarkableness of each milestone – she was always ready for the next responsibility, the next challenge, and the next opportunity to serve. I admired Kay Granger the moment I met her. She carried herself with an unmistakable grace, but behind her regal appearance was a razor-sharp tenacity that commanded any room. Kay demanded respect, and she got it from everyone she ever interacted with. Whip-smart and Texas tough, she had a presence that could settle any debate with little more than a look. I was lucky enough to know her personally and professionally through our work serving together in Republican leadership. So, I can attest with firsthand knowledge that ‘Don’t mess with Texas’ was more than a motto when it came to Kay. I know it well because I lost to her when we both sought the chairmanship of the Appropriations Committee previously. After that, our friendship and mutual respect didn’t change for one another. In fact, she named me to be her Vice Chair. Her mentorship and guidance were large parts of my own committee journey and helped prepare me for the privilege of succeeding her as Chairman. On the Appropriations Committee, Kay was known as a fiscal conservative, a defense hawk, and a hard – but fair – negotiator. Ever proud of her Texas roots, Granger ferociously fought for the interests of the Lone Star State. Her colleagues on both sides of the aisle always respected her professionalism, her good humor, her unfailing civility, and her willingness to strike a deal. Indeed, she and the first woman to Chair the Appropriations Committee, Nita Lowey of New York, were fast friends. They were partners who set the gold standard of how to achieve bipartisan consensus. Their portraits above our dais today remind us of the example they set and the responsibility we inherit. I will miss my friend Kay Granger. She set an unmatched standard of excellence, civility, professionalism, and dedication to duty that few can match – and no one will ever exceed. My thoughts and prayers are with Kay’s family, friends, and many admirers. We have lost a great lioness of the House, and I have lost a dear friend to whom I shall always be indebted.

It was an honor to present Carol Arbour of Pawcatuck with the medals her father, Harold Gley, earned while serving our country during World War II. Private First Class Gley served in the U.S. Army from 1944 to 1945, his awards include the Bronze Star Medal, Good Conduct Medal, European-African-Middle Eastern Campaign Medal with 2 bronze service stars for three battle campaigns he fought in, and the World War II Victory Medal. Mrs. Arbour was also presented with her father’s Combat Infantryman Badge and Honorable Service Lapel Button for service in WWII. Like so many veterans, Harold’s service records were lost in the 1973 National Personnel Records Center fire. I am glad that my office was able to recover the recognition he earned more than 80 years ago and present his family with a shadow box honoring his service.

Four years ago today, the bipartisan PACT Act became law, delivering the largest expansion of veterans’ health care and benefits in decades. Since then, veterans across the country, including thousands in Connecticut, have claimed their benefits. Here in eastern Connecticut, at Veterans Rally Point in Norwich, and the annual "Veterans Stand Down” event at Quinebaug Valley Community College, hundreds of deserving Veterans were enrolled in the new program.  For veterans exposed to burn pits, Agent Orange, and other toxic substances during their service, the PACT Act delivers the care our veterans deserve and keeps our promise to provide them and their families.

C001063.text: I announced approximately $1.212 billion in federal funding for five major South Texas construction projects alongside Hector Garza, President of National Border Patrol Council 2455; Sergio Moreno, National Border Patrol Council Executive Board Member; the Border Patrol Union; City of Laredo Mayor Dr. Victor D. Treviño; State Representative Richard Raymond; City of Laredo Council Members; and Jerry Garza, Webb County Judge-Elect, and local trade leaders. These projects will strengthen border security, improve working conditions for our agents, and support the efficient movement of legitimate trade. This historic federal investment includes approximately $492 million for a new Laredo Sector Headquarters, more than $200 million to expand the C29 Checkpoint to 13 lanes, approximately $330 million for the Laredo Joint Processing Center, approximately $62 million for a new Laredo Air Branch, and approximately $128 million for a new Border Patrol Station in Freer. These projects will modernize facilities, strengthen operations, improve traffic flow, and support local construction activity and jobs. I’ve also worked to secure federal resources for fair overtime compensation for Border Patrol agents, workforce staffing, suicide prevention and wellness, and new border-security technology. These investments recognize that our border security mission depends on the men and women who carry it out every day. I’m grateful to our Border Patrol agents, union leadership, trade community, and local officials for their partnership and for continuing to share what South Texas needs. As Ranking Member of the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Homeland Security, I’ll continue fighting to bring federal resources back to TX-28, strengthen our border, and keep our economy moving.

I announced that I secured $950,000 in Community Project Funding for the City of Laredo Animal Shelter expansion. This funding marks an important step forward in the federal funding process and will help expand the shelter’s capacity to care for animals across Laredo. These federal dollars will help expand the shelter, create additional clinical and service space, improve infrastructure, and purchase equipment for examinations, vaccinations, and spay and neuter services. This investment will help provide more animals with preventive care, reduce overcrowding, support public health and safety, and give more dogs and cats a second chance at finding a loving home. I’m grateful to the Laredo Animal Care Services team, rescue partners, foster families, volunteers, veterinarians, and city leaders who work every day to care for animals in our community. I’ll continue working to bring federal resources back to TX-28 and support the people who are making Laredo a safer, stronger, and more compassionate community.

D000600.text: Tengo el corazón lleno de profunda gratitud al unirme a la celebración del renombramiento de la Escuela Primaria de Hialeah en memoria de mi hermano, Lincoln Diaz-Balart. Lincoln vivió con un compromiso inquebrantable con el servicio público y la convicción de que cada niño merece la oportunidad de aprender y prosperar. Cada estudiante que cruce estas puertas verá su nombre, y espero que se sienta inspirado por los valores con los que él vivió: compasión, integridad y una dedicación a hacer el bien público ayudando a muchas personas. Estoy agradecido de que la Escuela Primaria Lincoln Diaz-Balart de Hialeah permanezca como un tributo duradero a su legado, recordándonos a todos el poder que cada uno de nosotros tiene para hacer la diferencia en la vida de los demás. La gran ciudad de Hialeah y sus residentes siempre ocuparon un lugar especial en el corazón de Lincoln. Él compartía un vínculo especial con esta comunidad que le eligió 9 veces al Congreso. Él comprendía las esperanzas, los desafíos y los sueños de Hialeah de una manera profundamente personal y apreciaba a su gente. Uno de los mayores honores de la vida de Lincoln fue haber sido la voz de los residentes de Hialeah en Washington durante 18 años. En nombre de toda nuestra familia quiero expresar mi más sincero agradecimiento a todos los que hicieron posible este honor, en especial quiero agradecer al miembro de la Junta Escolar Dan Espino por su arduo trabajo en este esfuerzo. Estamos profundamente agradecidos por la forma en que nos han acogido mientras honran el legado de Lincoln.

It fills my heart with profound gratitude to join the celebration of the renaming of Hialeah Elementary School in memory of my late brother, Lincoln Diaz-Balart. Lincoln lived with an unwavering commitment to public service and the belief that every child deserves the chance to learn and thrive.  As each student steps through these doors, they will see his name and, I hope, feel inspired by the values he lived—compassion, integrity, and a dedication to doing the public good by helping many. I am grateful that the Lincoln Diaz-Balart Hialeah Elementary School will stand as a lasting tribute to his legacy, reminding us all of the power that each one of us has to make a difference in the lives of others. The great city of Hialeah and its residents always held a special place in Lincoln’s heart. He shared a special bond with this community, who 9 times elected him to Congress. He understood the hopes, challenges, and dreams of Hialeah in a deeply personal way, and he cherished its people. It was one of the great honors of Lincoln’s life to be the voice of the residents of Hialeah in Washington for 18 years.  On behalf of our entire family, I want to express my heartfelt gratitude to everyone who made this honor possible. I especially want to thank School Board Member Dan Espino for his hard work on this effort. We are profoundly grateful for the way you have embraced us while honoring Lincoln’s legacy.

For 250 years, our great experiment has faltered, flourished, evolved, and progressed. The American experience is ever-changing and as diverse as the people who call this country home. But one thing has remained constant – the idea of America has always been a beacon of hope. Protecting this country and the ideals and values it was founded on takes work. Democracy is demanding. It takes dedication and principle. And it takes the resounding belief that upholding those ideals and values is worth the fight because America is bigger than any one person. Because liberty can only truly endure when it is paired with responsibility, virtue, and a commitment to put public good ahead of personal ambition. Today, we celebrate the moment when our founding fathers openly declared that creating this country, based in liberty, was a necessity in the face of tyranny. Their legacy is that leadership requires courage when it’s difficult, integrity when no one is watching, and a willingness to put country above self. We must remember that our duty is not merely to the next election, but to the next generation. That should be the challenge for all Americans as we look forward to another 250 years. From Massachusetts, where the fight for freedom first began, I wish you a happy 4th of July. God Bless America always, God Bless all who call her home, and God Bless our courageous men and women in uniform who continue the fight for liberty today.

On Monday, our office suffered an unimaginable loss. Chris Matthews, my District Outreach and Communications Director, passed away unexpectedly. If any one of you begin to lose faith in our country, remember Chris Matthews. Remember he was without question one of the Commonwealth’s sharpest political minds – a generational talent. Remember that he was more than a Congressional aide. He took the belief that through our actions we all can bring needed change and brought it with him on many interstate bus rides to canvas distant pivotal states and to the doors of the families he inspired. Remember through his example that public service is a genuinely noble vocation. As a trusted member of our office, he helped countless veterans, families, and those who could not advocate for themselves. Those of us privileged to have worked with him for over fifteen years will remember his laugh and his wry, often biting, humor – contrasting the way things are to the way they could be. We will always remember his authentic belief that in this country, people can bring about progress and meaningful change. It was real to him and his sincerity shown through. Chris was a genuinely good person. He was family to all of us, and we are devastated by his loss, particularly at such a young age. Our thoughts and prayers are with Molly and Eli and the many who loved him. Though we wish we had more time with him, his memory will continue to give us faith that one person can significantly make better the lives of those around him.

I recently visited Neil and Michelle Franke’s farm in Perry County to tour their operation and hear firsthand about the challenges facing Missouri livestock producers. With around 500 head of cattle, the Frankes have built a successful operation on land that has been in their family since the late 1800s. We discussed the regulatory and insurance challenges they face and what Washington can do to help Missouri farmers continue to grow and succeed. Last year, I was proud to deliver major wins for Missouri agriculture in the Working Families Tax Cuts, including making the 20% small business deduction permanent and allowing farmers to immediately expense the cost of new equipment. Our farmers feed and fuel our nation, which is exactly why I’m committed to keep fighting to ensure Missouri farm families can thrive for generations to come.

Enjoyed visiting Mesta Meadows Farm in Bollinger County this week to see the operation firsthand and hear how this family has built a business that reaches customers in all 50 states and more than a dozen countries. The family has spent the last decade building today’s operation, raising sheep, cattle, goats, pigs, and poultry. They sell direct to consumers through farmers markets in St. Louis and Cape Girardeau, a store on the property, and online, moving products like raw milk, wool, and roughly 1,500 pints of ice cream a week with a team of just three full-time employees. Thanks to the Working Families Tax Cuts, Mesta Meadows and farms like it can count on permanent 100% immediate expensing and a permanent small business deduction, making it easier to reinvest in their operation and keep pace as their business grows. I’ll keep fighting for policies that help Missouri farm families like this one continue to thrive.

On a six-acre farm just outside New Hope, Jessica Zander has built something our community should be deeply proud of. Helping Friendly Farm in Solebury Township is a place where children, families, and individuals with disabilities can grow, connect, and feel fully welcomed. For more than 20 years, Jessica has devoted her life to individuals with special needs, helping them build confidence, skills, and foster positive opportunities and connection. Her path began with my longtime partners at AmeriCorps, where she served as a special education teacher. From there, she continued serving in specialized mental health and special education programs, and brought therapeutic yoga and meditation to children with special needs. As a mother of children with complex medical needs, Jessica understands what so many families carry every day—the appointments, questions, advocacy, trials and tribulations, and constant search for places where their loved ones will be met with patience, respect, and understanding. So, Jessica created that place. At Helping Friendly Farm, visitors of all ages and backgrounds can pet donkeys, sit with goats, explore a sensory barn, plant seeds, play on swings, spend time in nature, and connect with animals raised to be gentle and familiar with wheelchairs and adaptive devices. It is not clinical. It is not overwhelming. It is warm, intentional, evidence-based, and full of joy, compassion, and a place where all people are seen not for what limits them, but for all they are capable of becoming. Her work reflects the kind of mission I will always fight for: ensuring that children, families, caregivers, and individuals with disabilities are seen, supported, included, and given every opportunity to thrive. Please join me in thanking and applauding Jessica and the entire HFF team for creating such an extraordinary place in our community—a true Hometown hero!

🚨 The Senate should not delay the SNAP state benefit cost-share requirement. States make more than $10 billion in erroneous SNAP payments every year, and the national payment error rate has nearly doubled since 2019. The problem is only getting worse. The One Big Beautiful Bill brings SNAP in line with other federally funded, state-administered programs, requiring states with the highest payment error rates to have skin in the game by sharing a modest portion of benefit costs. That's commonsense accountability, stronger program integrity, and better stewardship of taxpayer dollars. With our national debt exceeding $39 trillion, we must stay committed to fiscal responsibility—not cave to Democrat demands to weaken accountability, waste taxpayer dollars meant to serve vulnerable Americans, and further fuel our debt crisis.

The fight for affordable housing is not just about the building you live in, it’s about the community you become a part of and the neighbors you look out for. Dawn is a resident of Sandhill Valley, a 55+ manufactured home neighborhood, and also works in her community as the program and activities director. She understands that building community takes work, and she’s not afraid to go the extra mile. When she’s not planning holiday celebrations or creating a wall to honor the veterans in the community, she’s giving her neighbors a ride to the airport and calling local nonprofits to fix their air conditioning unit. Not everyone needs a three-story house in a masterplan development. That’s why I fought to ensure the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act expanded financial access to manufactured housing loans and preserved grant funding to repair, preserve, and improve existing manufactured homes and communities. Nevadans need housing that’s safe, affordable, and among community. Home is where you make it and Dawn, Barbara, and Tony have made it at Sandhill Valley.

M001204.text: Our Gold Star Families deserve our enduring gratitude and respect. Behind every fallen hero is a family who carries their memory, their legacy, and their sacrifice forward. It was an honor to spend time with Bob and Nick Sandri and remember Bob’s son, Sgt. Matthew J. Sandri of Shamokin. Matthew served as a paratrooper and Army medic with the 82nd Airborne Division and had been serving in Iraq since August 2003. On March 20, 2004, Matthew was killed in action from injuries sustained during an enemy rocket attack on the medical facility where he was serving near Fallujah, Iraq. He was just 24 years old. Matthew’s legacy of service continues more than two decades later, both in the military and within his own family. The Taylor-Sandri Medical Training Center at Fort Bragg bears his name alongside Lt. Col. Mark Taylor, who was killed in the same attack, and continues to train military medical personnel in lifesaving battlefield care. That same spirit of service lives on through Matthew’s cousin, Nick, who recently completed the police academy and joined the Shamokin Police Department, carrying forward his cousin’s commitment to serving others and his community. Earlier this summer, Bob and Nick asked if I could help deliver a letter to President Trump in Matthew’s memory. I was grateful to recently present them with President Trump’s thoughtful response to their family. The Sandri family’s story is a powerful reminder of the tremendous sacrifice borne by our Gold Star Families. We can never fully repay the debt we owe our fallen heroes or the families who carry their memories forward, but we can ensure their names, their service, and their sacrifice are never forgotten. May God bless the Sandri family, all of our Gold Star Families, and all those who have given their lives in defense of our nation.

I’m pleased to announce that the Department of Homeland Security has transferred the Socorro warehouses to the General Services Administration (GSA). This means the warehouses will be put up for sale and they will no longer be used by the federal government for detention purposes. The community of Socorro has been working on an economic development vision and plan to grow their economy while embracing their rich history. The community has also faced challenges with water, wastewater, and general infrastructure, making the purchase of these facilities for detention a terrible idea to begin with, threatening their ability to execute on their future plans and growth. My team and I have worked diligently to elevate these issues within DHS and ICE and ensure that the voices of our community were heard. My priority is to work with Socorro leadership to support our shared constituents and their needs. This news will help all of us focus on that path ahead instead of the greater challenges a massive detention facility would bring. I will continue to productively advocate for our community and what is in the best interests of all of us.

H001091.text: Thank you to Senator @ChuckGrassley and of course Mrs G. for joining me in Waterloo today to talk with independent pharmacists about challenges facing rural pharmacies and their patients. One thing everyone in the room agreed on: shady PBM practices are driving up costs for patients and squeezing independent pharmacies out of business. No Iowan should go to a pharmacy only to find out the medicine they need has doubled or tripled in price. We’ve made some progress on PBM reform — including forcing more transparency and preventing PBMs from profiting off higher drug costs, but we’ve got a long way to go to ensure middlemen aren’t driving up costs for Iowans.

C001129.text: On this day in history in 1981, IBM releases its version of a personal computer, or PC. IBM CEO Frank Cary gave William Lowe one month to develop a prototype for a PC that appealed to small businesses and consumers for $1,500. He was given a year to take it to market. The IBM PC became the industry standard as it was now possible to connect to a television, allowing users to manage text and play games. It improved business efficiency, drove the growth of the software industry, and brought computing into widespread use.

On this day in history in 1934, the nation’s most dangerous criminals arrived at Alcatraz. Converted into a maximum-security federal penitentiary in 1934, Alcatraz held notorious criminals such as Al Capone, George “Machine Gun” Kelly, and Robert Stroud, the “Birdman of Alcatraz.” The prison became infamous for escape attempts—most notably the 1962 breakout by Frank Morris and the Anglin brothers, which inspired the film Escape from Alcatraz. Due to high maintenance costs, Alcatraz closed in 1963 after housing over 1,500 inmates in its 29-year run.

On this day in history in 1776, news of America’s Declaration of Independence reached London. Dispatches from General Howe had finally crossed the Atlantic and arrived by horseback. On August 10, the London Gazette carried a short line confirming that the Continental Congress had declared the United Colonies “free and independent States.” What many in Britain had viewed as a colonial uprising was now an official war.
“Praise the Lord, all you nations; extol him, all you peoples. For great is his love toward us, and the faithfulness of the Lord endures forever. Praise the Lord.” — Psalm 117:1-2

On this day in history in 1782, George Washington created the Purple Heart during his time as the commander in chief of the Continental Army during the Revolutionary War. He awarded it to only three soldiers during the Revolutionary War. The purple badge allowed soldiers to pass guards without challenge and have their names recorded in the “Book of Merit.” The award was forgotten until it was reinstated on Washington’s 200th birthday in 1932. Today, the Purple Heart is awarded to soldiers who have been wounded, killed, or prisoners of war. It is the oldest American award for the armed forces.

RT by @RepMaloyUtah: On Pioneer Day, I had the opportunity to tour Beaver and see firsthand the devastating impact of both wildfire and flooding. Standing in those burned and flooded landscapes, talking with the Forest Service personnel, local leaders, and the people of Beaver one thing was crystal clear: forest management works. The difference between treated and untreated forest was visible. Areas that had been thinned or otherwise managed gave firefighters a chance. They slowed the fire, reduced its intensity, helped crews establish containment lines, and in some cases, stopped the fire altogether. In the overgrown, untreated areas, the fire burned hotter, moved faster, and left behind far greater destruction, burning an unprecedented 70,000 acres in two days. It's frustrating that while the United States is the world's largest importer of lumber and paper products, millions of acres of our own forests sit overcrowded and vulnerable to catastrophic wildfire. The boots-on-the-ground Forest Service personnel managing these forests know what needs to be done and want to actively manage these lands, but too often commonsense projects are delayed or stopped by endless litigation and opposition by environmentalists and bureaucrats in Washington D.C. That's why the Fix Our Forests Act deserves to move forward. The legislation passed the House with strong bipartisan support, but has been stalled in the Senate for 18 months. It needs to move forward. I'm grateful to Congresswoman Celeste Maloy for bringing us together to see this firsthand, and to the Trump Administration officials who came to Utah to witness these conditions on the ground. With the U.S. Forest Service headquarters coming to Utah, we have a tremendous opportunity to ensure the people making decisions about our forests are closer to the landscapes and communities they serve. Thank you to USDA's Michael Boren, Sam Crofts from the Bureau of Land Management, and Chairman Bruce Westerman of the House Natural Resources Committee for taking the time to be there and hear directly from those who have been impacted by this catastrophe. On Pioneer Day weekend, that lesson feels especially meaningful. The pioneers who settled this state understood that stewardship requires hard work, planning, and taking responsibility for the land we call home. We honor their legacy not by leaving our forests untouched until they burn and cause catastrophic damage, but by actively caring for them so they remain healthy for generations to come. The Beaver community continues to show incredible resilience. I was reminded why I'm so proud to be a Utahn. We face challenges head-on, we help our neighbors, and we don't shy away from doing the difficult work that's necessary to protect our communities and our public lands. @realDonaldTrump @RepMaloyUtah @RepWesterman @SenJohnCurtis @RepBurgessOwens @RepMikeKennedy @USDA @forestservice @Interior @BLMNational @NatResources @JStuartAdams @cralbrecht52 @BeaverCountyUT

S001201.text: ROAD TO 250: The Intelligence Behind Independence Some of the most important battles of the American Revolution were fought not with muskets, but with secrets. In Oyster Bay, Raynham Hall was home to Robert Townsend, a key member of George Washington’s Culper Spy Ring. Operating under the alias “Samuel Culper Jr.,” Townsend gathered critical intelligence from inside British-occupied New York and helped pass it through a secret network to Washington and the Continental Army. The Culper spies used aliases, coded messages, invisible ink, and an elaborate network of couriers to gather and transmit information while risking imprisonment or death if they were discovered. Their story is also a Long Island story. That’s why I introduced bipartisan legislation to establish the Washington Spy Ring National Historic Trail, recognizing the sites and communities that played a critical role in the Culper Ring and America’s fight for independence. As we continue to celebrate America’s 250th birthday, we should remember not only the famous names of the Revolution, but the secret patriots whose courage and ingenuity helped make independence possible.

I was honored to welcome my friend, the Ambassador of Hungary to the United States, @_SzabolcsTakacs to Haralson County today. In the late 1800s, dozens of Hungarian families moved from Pennsylvania's coal mines to Haralson County to establish a wine-making community.  They named their village Budapest after the Hungarian capital, and planted vineyards across the surrounding hillsides.  After Prohibition was enacted in the 1920s, many of the families left, and all that remains from that era is a home which once served as a Catholic rectory and the historic Budapest cemetery.  Today, we visited both. Ambassador Takács' visit is a special moment in Haralson County's rich history, and I am grateful for the incredible support the Haralson County Historical Society, the Hungarian Community Church of Georgia, the Dogwood Hills team, and local officials and community leaders provided to facilitate this meaningful event. Thank you, Ambassador Takács, for visiting Georgia's 3rd Congressional District, and thank you for strengthening the relationship between Hungary and the United States of America! @HungaryinUSA

RT by @RepBrianJack: Grateful to join the amazing Steve Gradick of WLPP and @RepBrianJack in Carrollton, Georgia yesterday for a fun long chat on all things America, agriculture, and saving our country. We announced the finalized Cooperative Interstate Shipment (CIS) agreement, giving qualifying Georgia state-inspected meat processors the opportunity to ship USDA-labeled products across state lines. This is a tremendous victory for Georgia's farmers, ranchers, and small meat processors. Yesterday, Georgia became one of only a handful of states participating in the Cooperative Interstate Shipment Program—allowing qualifying state-inspected meat processors to ship USDA-labeled products nationwide. For too long, a handful of massive processors have dominated the market, putting family-owned processors at a disadvantage. This is another step toward expanding opportunity, strengthening rural America, increasing competition, and rebuilding America's food production capacity. Under Biden, the United States flipped from net agricultural exporter to net importer. Four years of weakness turned a historic American strength into a strategic vulnerability. We’re fixing that. Food security is national security. Thank you Georgia!!! 🥩🐂🇺🇸

WORLD_UK_PM.text: Growth demands a relentless focus on the future. This would be like Blair railing against Macmillan, or me blaming Jim Callaghan for the challenges of the 2020s. The emphasis on the past is even more concerning given that Burnham has abolished the government department most focused on the future. WORLD_GERMANY_CHANCELLOR.text: Die Sicherheitslage hat sich verändert. Deshalb müssen unsere Nachrichtendienste Bedrohungen früher erkennen und, falls erforderlich, aktiv handeln können, um Deutschland besser zu schützen. Wir stärken ihre Fähigkeiten mit klaren rechtsstaatlichen Grenzen und starker Kontrolle.

Wir bauen die Altersvorsorge weiter um – hin zur Vorsorge von Anfang an. Mit der Frühstartrente statten wir Kinder ab sechs Jahren mit Startkapital für ihre private Altersvorsorge aus. Sie profitieren früh von den Chancen des Kapitalmarkts und wir stärken die Altersvorsorge.

Sigo con consternación las noticias sobre el grave terremoto en Colombia. Mis condolencias a las víctimas y sus familias. A los numerosos hombres y mujeres que prestan ayuda les deseo mucha fuerza en las próximas horas y días.

Mit Bestürzung verfolge ich die Nachrichten über das schwere Erdbeben in Kolumbien. Mein Mitgefühl gilt den Opfern und ihren Familien. Den vielen Helferinnen und Helfern wünsche ich viel Kraft in den nächsten Stunden und Tagen.

Der Schutz der EU-Außengrenzen ist entscheidend für die Bekämpfung illegaler Migration. Ich unterstütze die spanische Absicht, die illegalen Migranten nicht auf den europäischen Kontinent zu lassen. Die Rückkehrverordnung der EU muss nun unverzüglich umgesetzt werden.

On World Elephant Day, we celebrate the majestic elephant which has remained an integral part of India’s ecological heritage. It is gladdening that India is home to over 60% of the world’s wild Asian elephants. Our nation has 33 Elephant Reserves, which provide habitats for elephants and strengthen our efforts towards their long-term conservation. We are also proud of all forest personnel, scientists, veterinarians, mahouts and the local communities who are integral to all such efforts.

WORLD_FRANCE_PRESIDENT.text: Face au terrible séisme qui a frappé la Colombie, j’adresse, au nom de la France, mes pensées les plus sincères au peuple colombien. Je pense aux victimes, à leurs familles, aux blessés et à toutes celles et ceux qui ont été touchés par cette catastrophe. Notre solidarité va également aux équipes de secours et à tous ceux qui œuvrent, avec courage, pour venir en aide aux populations sinistrées. Dans cette épreuve, la Colombie peut compter sur notre amitié et notre soutien.

Félicitations à Demi Vollering, vainqueure du Tour de France Femmes ! À chaque étape, un même engouement et une ferveur populaire pour faire vivre cette grande fête du cyclisme mondial. Une course qui rassemble, une fierté française.

À Kyiv et dans sa région, la Russie a une nouvelle fois choisi de cibler des civils. Cette politique de terreur, menée à coups de missiles et de drones, est inacceptable. Chaque nouvelle attaque renforce une évidence : la Russie doit payer le prix de son agression et répondre de ses crimes. Aux côtés de l’Ukraine, nous ne céderons ni à la lassitude ni à l’intimidation. L’Union européenne et ses partenaires continueront d’accroître la pression sur la Russie, notamment par de nouvelles sanctions, tout en renforçant le soutien militaire à l’Ukraine afin qu’elle puisse se défendre et protéger sa population.
